question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

INGENUOUS
option_1: Cunning
option_2: Devious
option_3: Artless
option_4: Calculating
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Artless.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ingenuous (adjective) means innocent, frank and unsuspecting; free from guile or calculation. (सरल, निष्कपट)
◦ Example: Her ingenuous reply disarmed even the hostile members of the panel.

 

• Artless means exactly this — without cunning or deceit; naturally simple. (छल-रहित, भोला)
◦ Example: He answered with artless honesty, unaware of the trouble it would cause.

 

• Do not confuse ingenuous with ingenious, which means clever and inventive. The two words differ by a single letter but are unrelated in sense, and SSC exploits this pair regularly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Cunning (धूर्त): skilled in deception — an antonym.

 

• Option 2: Devious (कपटी): using underhand means to achieve an end — an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Calculating (स्वार्थपूर्ण गणना करने वाला): acting from cold self-interest — an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of ingenuous: naive, guileless, candid, unaffected, open.

 

• The noun forms differ too: ingenuousness (innocence) against ingenuity (inventiveness).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

PENURY
option_1: Affluence
option_2: Destitution
option_3: Indigence
option_4: Privation
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Affluence.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Penury (noun) means extreme poverty; the state of being utterly without means. (घोर निर्धनता)
◦ Example: The once prosperous family was reduced to penury within a decade.

 

• Its true opposite is affluence — an abundance of wealth and material comfort. (समृद्धि, सम्पन्नता)
◦ Example: The suburb is a byword for affluence.

 

• Options 2, 3 and 4 all denote poverty or want, so they are synonyms of the given word and may be eliminated as a group.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Destitution (नितांत अभाव): the state of lacking even the necessities of life — a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Indigence (दरिद्रता): poverty, neediness — a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Privation (अभाव, कष्ट): the lack of the basic comforts of life — a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of penury: opulence, prosperity, wealth, plenty, luxury.

 

• Note the adjective form penurious, which has two senses — very poor and, of a person, miserly.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

An Achilles heel
option_1: A wound that refuses to heal
option_2: A hasty retreat from a losing battle
option_3: A long and exhausting journey on foot
option_4: A single fatal weakness in an otherwise strong person or thing
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A single fatal weakness in an otherwise strong person or thing.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'An Achilles heel' means one vulnerable point in something otherwise strong and well defended. (एकमात्र कमजोर कड़ी)
◦ Example: Poor fielding has long been the Achilles heel of an otherwise formidable side.

 

• The phrase comes from Greek legend: the hero Achilles was made invulnerable everywhere except the heel by which his mother had held him, and it was there that the fatal arrow struck.

 

• The essential element is that the weakness is solitary and decisive — everything else about the subject is strong.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reads the word 'heel' as a literal injury and misses the figurative sense.

 

• Option 2 describes flight from battle, for which the idiom is 'to beat a retreat'.

 

• Option 3 would suit an expression such as 'a long haul'.

 

NOTE

 

• Other idioms drawn from classical legend: a Herculean task, to open a Pandora's box, a Trojan horse, the Midas touch, to clean the Augean stables.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To carry the can
option_1: To fetch water and supplies for a group
option_2: To take the blame for something, often on another's behalf
option_3: To be handed an unusually easy assignment
option_4: To obey an order without questioning it
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To take the blame for something, often on another's behalf.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'To carry the can' means to accept responsibility or blame for a failure, frequently one caused by somebody else. (दूसरों की गलती का दोष अपने सिर लेना)
◦ Example: When the scheme collapsed, the junior officer was left to carry the can.

 

• The expression is of military origin: the man given the menial duty of carrying the can was also the one blamed if anything went wrong with it.

 

• The idiom always implies blame, and usually undeserved blame — which is what separates it from the three distractors.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 takes 'carry the can' literally; idioms must never be read word by word.

 

• Option 3 reverses the sense — carrying the can is an unwelcome burden, not an easy task.

 

• Option 4 describes unquestioning obedience, for which the idiom would be 'to toe the line'.

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms of blame and responsibility: to be made a scapegoat, to take the rap, to face the music, to hold the baby, to pass the buck (the opposite — to shift blame to somebody else).

question: Which is the correct spelling of a word meaning 'about to happen at any moment'?
option_1: Imminent
option_2: Eminent
option_3: Iminent
option_4: Immenent
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Imminent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Imminent (adjective) means likely to occur at any moment; impending. (आसन्न, निकट)
◦ Example: The met office warned that a cyclone was imminent.

 

• The word begins with i and doubles the m: im-min-ent. It comes from Latin imminere, 'to overhang' — the idea of something looming just above.

 

• Eminent (Option 2) is a real word but an entirely different one — it means distinguished, famous, standing out. (प्रतिष्ठित)
◦ Example: An eminent jurist chaired the commission.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 3: Iminent — wrong; the m must be doubled.

 

• Option 4: Immenent — wrong; the second vowel is i, not e.

 

NOTE

 

• Complete the confusable set for the exam: imminent (about to happen), eminent (distinguished), immanent (existing within, inherent). All three are pronounced almost alike.

question: Choose the correct one-word substitution for: 'One who hates or distrusts humankind in general'.
option_1: Philanthropist
option_2: Anthropologist
option_3: Misogamist
option_4: Misanthrope
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Misanthrope.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A misanthrope is a person who dislikes and avoids humankind as a whole. (मानवद्वेषी)
◦ Example: Years of disappointment had turned the old scholar into a misanthrope.

 

• The word joins Greek misein ('to hate') and anthropos ('human being'). The abstract noun is misanthropy.

 

• The options are built from four Greek roots — miso- (hatred), philo- (love), anthropos (human being) and gamos (marriage). Since two options share miso-, it is the second element that decides: anthropos, not gamos.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Philanthropist (परोपकारी): one who loves humankind and gives generously to good causes — the direct opposite.

 

• Option 2: Anthropologist (मानवविज्ञानी): one who studies human societies and their development.

 

• Option 3: Misogamist (विवाह-विरोधी): one who hates the institution of marriage.

 

NOTE

 

• Build the family from the roots: miso- (hatred) gives misanthrope, misogamist, misoneism (hatred of novelty); philo- (love) gives philanthropist, bibliophile, philologist.

question: Choose the correct one-word substitution for: 'A person who is new to an activity or occupation'.
option_1: Veteran
option_2: Novice
option_3: Maestro
option_4: Doyen
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Novice.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A novice is a beginner; one who has just taken up an activity and has no experience of it. (नौसिखिया, नवागंतुक)
◦ Example: As a novice he made every mistake the manual warned against.

 

• The word comes from Latin novus, 'new' — the same root as novel and innovation.

 

• The other three options all denote long experience or mastery, so they are opposites of the required sense.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Veteran (अनुभवी व्यक्ति): one with long experience in a field.

 

• Option 3: Maestro (निपुण उस्ताद): a distinguished master, especially in music.

 

• Option 4: Doyen (वरिष्ठतम व्यक्ति): the senior-most and most respected member of a group or profession.

 

NOTE

 

• Other words for a beginner: tyro, neophyte, greenhorn, apprentice, fledgling.

question:
Select the appropriate word form:

 

The minister expressed his _____ with the slow pace of the relief work.
option_1: dissatisfy
option_2: dissatisfied
option_3: dissatisfaction
option_4: dissatisfying
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. dissatisfaction.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The blank follows the possessive adjective his and precedes the preposition with. That position can be filled only by a noun.

 

• Of the four forms offered, only dissatisfaction is a noun; it means the feeling of being displeased or discontented. (असंतोष)
◦ Example: He voiced his dissatisfaction with the quality of the materials.

 

• The completed sentence: The minister expressed his dissatisfaction with the slow pace of the relief work.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: dissatisfy — the base verb; a verb cannot follow a possessive adjective.

 

• Option 2: dissatisfied — the past participle used as an adjective, describing the person: *He was dissatisfied with the work.*

 

• Option 4: dissatisfying — the present participle used as an adjective, describing the thing that causes the feeling: *a dissatisfying result.*

 

NOTE

 

• The word family is worth memorising as a set: satisfy (verb) — satisfaction / dissatisfaction (noun) — satisfied / dissatisfied (adjective of the person) — satisfying / satisfactory (adjective of the thing) — satisfactorily (adverb).

question:
Select the correct option:

 

The scientist _____ discovery transformed modern medicine was never awarded the prize.
option_1: who
option_2: whose
option_3: whom
option_4: which
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. whose.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The blank stands immediately before the noun discovery and must show that the discovery belongs to the scientist. The relative pronoun that expresses possession is whose.

 

• Whose is the only relative pronoun that can be followed directly by a noun, and it may refer to people, animals or things alike.
◦ Example: This is the village whose water supply failed last summer.

 

• The completed sentence: The scientist whose discovery transformed modern medicine was never awarded the prize.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: who — the subject form; it would have to be followed by a verb, as in *the scientist who discovered ...*.

 

• Option 3: whom — the object form, used after a verb or preposition: *the scientist whom we honoured.*

 

• Option 4: which — used for things, not for a person, and it cannot show possession before a noun.

 

NOTE

 

• Quick test for who / whom / whose: substitute a personal pronoun — if he fits, use who; if him fits, use whom; if his fits, use whose.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The reason for his resignation (1)/ was because he had been (2)/ repeatedly passed over (3)/ for promotion. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'The reason ... was because' is a redundant construction. The word reason already states the cause, and because states it a second time. The correct link after 'the reason' is that.

 

• Part (2) must therefore read 'was that he had been'.

 

• The corrected sentence: The reason for his resignation was that he had been repeatedly passed over for promotion.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — 'the reason for' takes a noun phrase and is beyond objection.

 

• Part (3) is correct — passed over is the standard phrasal verb for being ignored in favour of somebody else; Part (4) is also sound.

 

NOTE

 

• Other redundancies of the same kind that SSC tests: return back, repeat again, revert back, cope up with, discuss about, more preferable, the reason is because.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The revised rules apply not only to (1)/ the permanent employees (2)/ but to the contractual staff also (3)/ in all the field offices. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (3).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'Not only ... but also' is a correlative pair. The two halves must be placed symmetrically, each immediately before the element it introduces.

 

• Since part (1) reads 'not only to', part (3) must mirror it exactly as 'but also to the contractual staff'. Detaching also and pushing it to the end breaks the parallel structure.

 

• The corrected sentence: The revised rules apply not only to the permanent employees but also to the contractual staff in all the field offices.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) and Part (2) are correct; to is rightly placed after 'not only'. In the corrected version it is repeated after 'but also' — *'but also to the contractual staff'*.

 

• Part (4) is sound.

 

NOTE

 

• Other correlative pairs that must be kept parallel: either ... or, neither ... nor, both ... and, whether ... or, no sooner ... than, hardly ... when, such ... that.

question:
Change the following from active to passive.

 

The council will announce the results next week.
option_1: The results are announced by the council next week.
option_2: The results would be announced by the council next week.
option_3: The results will have been announced by the council next week.
option_4: The results will be announced by the council next week.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The results will be announced by the council next week.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The active sentence is in the simple future tense (will announce). The passive of the simple future is formed as:
◦ will be + past participle (V3)

 

• Steps applied here:
◦ The object the results becomes the subject.
◦ will announce → will be announced.
◦ The subject the council becomes the agent introduced by by.

 

• The tense marker next week confirms that the future must be preserved.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 shifts the sentence into the simple present passive.

 

• Option 2 replaces will with would, turning a plain future into a conditional or a reported statement.

 

• Option 3 gives the future perfect passive, which corresponds to the active 'will have announced'.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember that shall/will + be + V3 is the only correct future passive; forms such as 'will being announced' or 'will been announced' do not exist.

question:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

The main gates are to be closed at nine o'clock by the security staff.
option_1: The security staff should have closed the main gates at nine o'clock.
option_2: The main gates close at nine o'clock for the security staff.
option_3: The security staff have closed the main gates at nine o'clock.
option_4: The security staff are to close the main gates at nine o'clock.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The security staff are to close the main gates at nine o'clock.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The structure 'be + to be + past participle' is the passive of the 'be to' construction, which expresses an arrangement, instruction or obligation.

 

• Its active counterpart keeps the same construction with the plain infinitive:
◦ Passive: The forms are to be submitted by the candidates. → Active: The candidates are to submit the forms.

 

• Applying this here, the agent the security staff becomes the subject and are to be closed becomes are to close, with the main gates as the object.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 introduces should have closed, which implies a duty that was not in fact performed.

 

• Option 2 removes the agent altogether and makes the gates close by themselves.

 

• Option 3 replaces the arrangement with the present perfect, reporting a completed act.

 

NOTE

 

• The 'be to' construction is common in official English — *The report is to be filed by Friday* — and its active form must retain 'is/are to', not be replaced by 'must' or 'should'.

question:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word.

 

The lorries carried limestone from the quarry on the hillside.
option_1: The abandoned quarry had slowly filled with rainwater.
option_2: The falcon circled patiently above its quarry.
option_3: Blasting at the quarry began soon after dawn.
option_4: The quarry supplied all the stone for the new bridge.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The falcon circled patiently above its quarry.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word identical in spelling and pronunciation to another but carrying an entirely different meaning. (समनामी शब्द)

 

• In the given sentence quarry means an open pit from which stone is extracted. The question therefore asks for the sentence in which the same word carries a different meaning.

 

• Option 2 uses quarry to mean an animal or bird being hunted; prey. The falcon and the verb 'circled' fix this second sense beyond doubt.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1, Option 3 and Option 4 all use quarry in the same mining sense as the highlighted word, so none of them qualifies as a homonym.

 

• The two senses have separate origins: the stone-pit quarry comes from Latin quadrare ('to square'), while the hunted quarry comes from Old French cuiree, the portion of the kill given to the hounds.

 

NOTE

 

• Keep the three terms distinct: homonyms are alike in spelling and sound (quarry, tender, spell); homophones sound alike but are spelt differently (sight/site, principal/principle, stationary/stationery); homographs are spelt alike but may be pronounced differently (lead, tear, minute).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

He has joined the company last month and is still under training.
option_1: has been joining
option_2: had joined
option_3: joined
option_4: was joining
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. joined.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The present perfect (has joined) can never be used with an adverbial that names a finished point of past time. Expressions such as last month, yesterday, in 2019, an hour ago demand the simple past.

 

• Since the sentence contains 'last month', the verb must be joined.
◦ Wrong: He has joined the company last month.
◦ Right: He joined the company last month.

 

• The corrected sentence: He joined the company last month and is still under training.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: has been joining — 'join' denotes a single completed act and does not take a continuous form in this sense.

 

• Option 2: had joined — the past perfect needs a second, later past action to relate to; there is none here.

 

• Option 4: was joining — the past continuous would suggest an action in progress, not a completed appointment.

 

NOTE

 

• The present perfect is correct with indefinite time expressions: just, already, yet, ever, never, recently, so far, since 2019, for two years.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Unless you do not submit the form before Friday, you will lose your claim.
option_1: Unless you submit
option_2: Unless you will submit
option_3: Until you do not submit
option_4: Unless you would submit
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Unless you submit.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Unless already carries a negative sense — it means 'if ... not'. Adding another negative inside the clause produces a double negative and reverses the intended meaning.

 

• The clause must therefore be written in the affirmative: 'Unless you submit the form before Friday', which is equivalent to *'If you do not submit the form before Friday'*.

 

• Note also that a clause of condition or time takes the present tense for future meaning, never 'will' or 'would'.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Unless you will submit — 'will' is not used in an if/unless clause referring to the future.

 

• Option 3: Until you do not submit — until marks time, not condition, and the negative is again redundant.

 

• Option 4: Unless you would submit — 'would' is equally inadmissible in the conditional clause.

 

NOTE

 

• Words that are already negative and must not be paired with another negative: unless, until, lest, seldom, hardly, scarcely, barely, nor. — *Take care lest you fall* (not 'lest you should not fall').

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

No sentence survives translation unchanged, and the honest translator begins by admitting it. A word carries not only a meaning but a history: the company it has kept, the quarrels it has settled, the jokes it has been used in. None of that freight can be loaded on to the corresponding word in another language, because the corresponding word has been living a different life. The translator's task is therefore not the mechanical one of substitution but the far harder one of deciding, again and again, what to lose.

 

That decision is never neutral. To render an ancient formal compound into plain English is to make the text sound accessible; to render the same compound into Latinate abstraction is to make it sound learned and remote. Neither is a distortion of the original in any simple sense — the original is capable of both readings — but each produces a different author for a different audience. The translator's invisibility, so often praised, is thus something of a fiction: the smoother the translation, the more completely the choices behind it have been concealed.

 

The consequences reach well beyond literature. Legal texts translated between languages of unequal power tend to acquire the categories of the stronger language, and a right that had no exact name in the weaker one may quietly cease to exist in the translated version. Scientific vocabulary, borrowed wholesale, brings with it assumptions that the borrowing culture never had occasion to examine. In each case the translation does not merely report a meaning; it settles one.

 

None of this argues for abandoning translation, which remains the only means by which most of the world's writing reaches most of its readers. It argues rather for reading translations as translations — as documents with an author of their own, made at a particular moment for a particular readership, and open to being made differently. A reader who remembers this loses a certain innocence and gains something better: the ability to ask, of any translated sentence, what it might have said instead.

 

Which of the following best encapsulates the primary thesis of the passage?
option_1: Translation is never neutral substitution but a series of choices that themselves shape meaning.
option_2: Translation should be avoided wherever the original language can be learnt instead.
option_3: Translation is a mechanical exercise that can be perfected with better dictionaries.
option_4: Translation matters chiefly in literature and rarely elsewhere.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Translation is never neutral substitution but a series of choices that themselves shape meaning.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first paragraph rejects the mechanical view outright: the translator's task is 'not the mechanical one of substitution but the far harder one of deciding, again and again, what to lose.'

 

• The second paragraph states the consequence — 'That decision is never neutral' — and the third shows the same choices settling meanings in law and science: 'the translation does not merely report a meaning; it settles one.'

 

• A thesis statement must cover the whole argument, and only Option 1 joins the rejection of mechanical substitution to the claim that the choices shape meaning.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 is contradicted by the final paragraph, which calls translation 'the only means by which most of the world's writing reaches most of its readers'.

 

• Option 3 is the very view the passage sets out to refute.

 

• Option 4 reverses the third paragraph, which insists that 'the consequences reach well beyond literature'.

 

NOTE

 

• In thesis questions, the correct option usually mirrors the passage's own 'not X but Y' structure; locate that sentence first.

What is implied by the statement that none of a word's 'freight' can be loaded on to the corresponding word in another language?
option_1: Translated books are physically heavier than the originals.
option_2: Long words are the hardest to translate accurately.
option_3: The accumulated associations a word has acquired cannot be carried across into another language.
option_4: Words in different languages never share any meaning at all.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The accumulated associations a word has acquired cannot be carried across into another language.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The metaphor is explained by the sentence just before it: a word carries 'not only a meaning but a history: the company it has kept, the quarrels it has settled, the jokes it has been used in.' That history is the freight.

 

• The reason given is that 'the corresponding word has been living a different life' — it has accumulated a different set of associations of its own.

 

• The image is therefore about connotation and history, not about physical weight or word length.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 takes the cargo metaphor literally.

 

• Option 2 introduces word length, which the passage never mentions.

 

• Option 4 overstates the case; the passage says the freight cannot be transferred, not that no meaning at all is shared.

 

NOTE

 

• For metaphor questions, the literal reading and the exaggerated reading are the two standard traps; the answer is normally the moderate paraphrase.

Scientific vocabulary, borrowed wholesale, brings with it assumptions that the borrowing culture never had occasion to examine. In each case the translation does not merely report a meaning; it settles one.

 

None of this argues for abandoning translation, which remains the only means by which most of the world's writing reaches most of its readers. It argues rather for reading translations as translations — as documents with an author of their own, made at a particular moment for a particular readership, and open to being made differently. A reader who remembers this loses a certain innocence and gains something better: the ability to ask, of any translated sentence, what it might have said instead.

 

What does the passage say about the translator's much-praised 'invisibility'?
option_1: It is the highest achievement a translator can aim at.
option_2: It is a fiction, because a smoother translation conceals its choices more completely.
option_3: It is impossible in legal and scientific texts but possible in literature.
option_4: It results from the translator's refusal to make any choices at all.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. It is a fiction, because a smoother translation conceals its choices more completely.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states: 'The translator's invisibility, so often praised, is thus something of a fiction: the smoother the translation, the more completely the choices behind it have been concealed.'

 

• The point is not that a smooth translation contains no choices, but that it hides them — an argument that turns the usual praise on its head.

 

• The preceding sentences supply the ground: the same compound may be rendered plainly or abstractly, and 'each produces a different author for a different audience.'

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 repeats the conventional praise that the passage is questioning.

 

• Option 3 invents a distinction between text types that the passage does not draw at this point.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the argument, which insists that choices are always made — only concealed.

 

NOTE

 

• Watch for the word 'thus': it marks the conclusion the author draws from the preceding illustration, and such sentences are the usual source of comprehension keys.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

No sentence survives translation unchanged, and the honest translator begins by admitting it. A word carries not only a meaning but a history: the company it has kept, the quarrels it has settled, the jokes it has been used in. None of that freight can be loaded on to the corresponding word in another language, because the corresponding word has been living a different life. The translator's task is therefore not the mechanical one of substitution but the far harder one of deciding, again and again, what to lose.

 

That decision is never neutral. To render an ancient formal compound into plain English is to make the text sound accessible; to render the same compound into Latinate abstraction is to make it sound learned and remote. Neither is a distortion of the original in any simple sense — the original is capable of both readings — but each produces a different author for a different audience. The translator's invisibility, so often praised, is thus something of a fiction: the smoother the translation, the more completely the choices behind it have been concealed.

 

The consequences reach well beyond literature. Legal texts translated between languages of unequal power tend to acquire the categories of the stronger language, and a right that had no exact name in the weaker one may quietly cease to exist in the translated version. Scientific vocabulary, borrowed wholesale, brings with it assumptions that the borrowing culture never had occasion to examine. In each case the translation does not merely report a meaning; it settles one.

 

None of this argues for abandoning translation, which remains the only means by which most of the world's writing reaches most of its readers. It argues rather for reading translations as translations — as documents with an author of their own, made at a particular moment for a particular readership, and open to being made differently. A reader who remembers this loses a certain innocence and gains something better: the ability to ask, of any translated sentence, what it might have said instead.

 

According to the passage, what may happen when legal texts are translated between languages of unequal power?
option_1: The weaker language gradually acquires new legal categories of its own.
option_2: Both languages are enriched by an exchange of legal ideas.
option_3: The translation becomes legally invalid in both jurisdictions.
option_4: A right with no exact name in the weaker language may quietly disappear from the translated version.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A right with no exact name in the weaker language may quietly disappear from the translated version.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states: such texts 'tend to acquire the categories of the stronger language, and a right that had no exact name in the weaker one may quietly cease to exist in the translated version.'

 

• The direction of influence is therefore from the stronger language to the weaker, and the loss falls on whatever the stronger language has no category for.

 

• The author's summing-up applies directly to this example: 'the translation does not merely report a meaning; it settles one.'

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the direction of influence described in the passage.

 

• Option 2 describes a mutual enrichment that the passage does not claim here.

 

• Option 3 raises legal validity, a matter the passage never discusses.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the passage's vocabulary of concealment — 'quietly', 'concealed', 'invisibility' — all of it marking losses and choices that occur without anyone noticing.

What does the author mean by urging readers to read 'translations as translations'?
option_1: To read them only after mastering the original language.
option_2: To compare every translated sentence with the original word by word.
option_3: To treat them as authored documents made for a particular readership and capable of being made differently.
option_4: To distrust translations entirely and rely on summaries instead.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To treat them as authored documents made for a particular readership and capable of being made differently.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrase is defined in the passage itself: translations should be read 'as documents with an author of their own, made at a particular moment for a particular readership, and open to being made differently.'

 

• The benefit the author claims follows immediately: such a reader gains 'the ability to ask, of any translated sentence, what it might have said instead.'

 

• The instruction is therefore about how to read, not about avoiding translations or checking them against the original.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 would make translation useless to the very readers the passage says it serves.

 

• Option 2 describes a word-by-word collation, which the passage never recommends — indeed it denies that word-for-word correspondence is possible.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the opening of the final paragraph: 'None of this argues for abandoning translation.'

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage repeats a phrase and then expands it with a dash or a colon, the expansion is almost always the wording of the correct option.

question:
Select the correct option for the Direct Speech conversion of the sentence below.

 

The guard forbade us to enter the restricted area after sunset.
option_1: The guard said to us, “I forbid you that you enter the restricted area after sunset.”
option_2: The guard said to us, “You did not enter the restricted area after sunset.”
option_3: The guard said to us, “Do not let them enter the restricted area after sunset.”
option_4: The guard said to us, “Do not enter the restricted area after sunset.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The guard said to us, “Do not enter the restricted area after sunset.”

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb forbade, followed by 'us to enter', marks the original as a negative command. Restoring the direct form requires three changes:
◦ forbade becomes said to;
◦ the pattern forbade + object + to-infinitive returns to the negative imperative, 'Do not + verb';
◦ the words are enclosed in inverted commas.

 

• The listeners are us, so in the direct form the command is addressed to you (understood), and no pronoun change beyond that is needed.

 

• The reconstructed sentence: The guard said to us, “Do not enter the restricted area after sunset.”

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps the reporting verb inside the quotation and uses an unidiomatic 'forbid ... that' construction.

 

• Option 2 turns a prohibition into a statement about the past.

 

• Option 3 redirects the command at a third party, whereas the guard was addressing us.

 

NOTE

 

• Reporting verbs for commands and their direct forms: ordered/commanded → plain imperative; forbade → 'Do not ...'; requested → 'Please ...'; advised → 'You should ...'; warned → 'Be careful ...'

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

The stranger said to me, “Can you tell me where the post office is?”
option_1: The stranger asked me whether I could tell him where the post office was.
option_2: The stranger asked me can I tell him where the post office is.
option_3: The stranger asked me whether could I tell him where was the post office.
option_4: The stranger said me if I can tell him where the post office was.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The stranger asked me whether I could tell him where the post office was.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Two questions are nested here, and both must lose their interrogative order.
◦ The outer yes/no question takes the connective whether (or 'if'), and Can you becomes I could.
◦ The inner wh- question keeps where as its connective, and the post office is becomes the post office was — subject before verb.

 

• The modal can backshifts to could, and the pronouns shift: you → I, me → him.

 

• The completed sentence: The stranger asked me whether I could tell him where the post office was.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps the interrogative order and the present tense throughout.

 

• Option 3 inverts both clauses — 'whether could I' and 'where was the post office' — which is precisely what indirect speech forbids.

 

• Option 4 uses the ungrammatical said me (it must be 'said to me' or 'told me') and fails to backshift can.

 

NOTE

 

• The single most reliable check in narration questions: in indirect speech there is no question mark and no inversion, however many questions the sentence contains.

question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a meaningful passage:

 

1. The pulp is then bleached and pressed into thin continuous sheets.
2. Paper-making begins with the shredding of wood or waste fibre into pulp.
3. The sheets are dried, trimmed and wound on to large reels.
4. Only at that stage does the paper become fit for printing.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 2-1-3-4.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 2 opens the paragraph: it names the process and states its first step. The word 'begins' settles its position beyond argument.

 

• Sentence 1 follows, marked by 'then' and by 'The pulp', which refers back to the pulp produced in sentence 2.

 

• Sentence 3 continues the sequence with 'The sheets', referring back to the sheets formed in sentence 1.

 

• Sentence 4 closes with the outcome, marked by 'Only at that stage', which presupposes all the earlier stages.

 

• The chain of definite noun phrases — pulp, sheets, that stage — fixes the order as 2-1-3-4.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (1-2-3-4) opens with 'The pulp' before the pulp has been made.

 

• Option 3 (2-3-1-4) puts the drying of the sheets before the sheets have been formed.

 

• Option 4 (3-1-2-4) begins in the middle of the process altogether.

 

NOTE

 

• In process passages, follow the chain of definite articles: each stage introduces a product that the next stage refers back to as 'the ...'. That chain alone usually settles the order.

question:
Rearrange the following sentences in correct order to make a logical passage.

 

1. It then measures how much of that water is actually billed to consumers.
2. Only when that figure is known can leakage be attacked at its source.
3. A water audit begins by measuring how much water enters the supply network.
4. The gap between the two figures is what engineers call unaccounted-for water.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 3-1-4-2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 3 opens the paragraph: it names the subject — a water audit — and gives its first measurement. The verb 'begins' fixes its place.

 

• Sentence 1 supplies the second measurement, marked by 'It then measures'; the pronoun It refers back to the audit of sentence 3.

 

• Sentence 4 can come only after both measurements, since 'the two figures' presupposes them.

 

• Sentence 2 concludes: 'that figure' refers to the unaccounted-for water just named, and 'Only when' signals the final consequence.

 

• The order is therefore first measure → second measure → the gap → the remedy: 3-1-4-2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (1-3-4-2) opens with 'It then measures', a pronoun with no antecedent and an adverb with nothing to follow.

 

• Option 3 (3-4-1-2) mentions 'the two figures' when only one has been given.

 

• Option 4 (4-3-1-2) begins with the gap before either figure has been introduced.

 

NOTE

 

• Three signposts settle most rearrangement questions: 'begins/first' marks the opening, a pronoun or demonstrative must follow its noun, and 'only when/therefore/hence' marks the close.
